Gilda Manfrin,
ideas

I work between education and consultancy in creative strategy for fashion and culture, connecting ideas, practice, and research.

Education Selected Projects About

The course is conceived as a full-time program, combining strategic, narrative, and creative development with a focus on contemporary visual communication, held by two different lecturers.

The course will treat:

Strategic research & content systems

  • a focus on strategic and conceptual research, narrative frameworks, and the development of a seasonal (6-month) communication plan and content projects design (with Gilda Manfrin);

Visual direction & presentation

  • notions of graphic design software (InDesign), presentation design, and art direction principles aimed at the conceptualization and visual direction of communication assets (with other lecturer).

The aim is to produce a single, integrated project that connects research, storytelling, and design — from concept to editorial and visual presentation. During the course, there will also be a joint lecture held in co-presence by both lecturers, dedicated to a shared review and coordination of the projects in view of their final refinement and presentation.

The first part of the course, while maintaining a practical approach and basing the entire experience on the making-of of an actual presentation and project design, will encourage reflection and an innovative approach to communication. In a landscape marked by content overproduction and the growing impact of digital technologies, we will focus on the role of brands as cultural agents and on the ability to design communication projects that combine clear strategies, effective storytelling, and coherent aesthetics.

Learning outcomes

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

  • develop a complete strategic presentation for a fashion brand, including research, objectives, storytelling, and editorial plan;
  • build an advanced and original narrative framework, inspired not only by personal taste and experience but also by contemporary research on culture and languages;
  • design content typologies and their distribution across formats and platforms;
  • learn to collaborate with different indications from multiple lecturers, working synergically towards a coherent final project;
  • be able to develop their own strategic proposal, structuring and presenting it independently with a clear and consistent approach.

Lesson program

The course is divided into two main phases.

The first part (1–8) introduces the main concepts, practices, and working methods through lectures and guided exercises. From lesson 9 onwards, students will work in groups to develop a proposal for a brand they wish to focus on, presenting their project pitch — including the reasons behind their choice and a first conceptual link with current and relevant cultural research. After the discussion with the lecturer and the class, they will proceed to the project realization phase, working in class through a series of workshops and revisions.

In addition to in-class work, the course includes curated educational outings — for example at Fondazione ICA, Fondazione Elpis, or Fondazione Sozzani — to connect the projects with contemporary artistic research and with specific cultural areas of the city. Guest lectures are also integrated: last year, for instance, a talk by Natalie Corre (Advance Copy) focused on values and purpose within brand communication.

\1

Lecture structure

  1. Introduction: background and context, with reference to the book Growing Independent Fashion Brands.
  2. Beyond conventional brand-building models: why traditional approaches no longer apply.
  3. Purpose as a strategic framework: definition of “purpose” and why it matters.
  4. Case studies: purpose in practice — examples of purpose‑driven brands and how values are applied:
    • Kowtow — 360 commitment to sustainability
    • Extreme Cashmere — representation (“For everybody, and every body”)
    • Sincerely Tommy — community building
    • Story Mfg. — transparency
  5. Wrap‑up / key learnings
  6. Q&A

Lecture summary

The lecture explored purpose-driven communication and the role of authenticity and transparency in building sustainable fashion brands. Through the experience of Advance Copy and selected case studies, it showed how clear values can be translated into consistent choices across design, communication, and production, balancing independence and scalability. The talk emphasised the importance of long-term thinking, proposing communication strategies that evolve over time and remain both commercially grounded and culturally conscious.

I personally find Natalia’s approach pragmatic, well-informed, and genuinely inspiring. Her book is a valuable resource for gaining a deeper understanding of many contemporary fashion brands, as well as the strategies and people behind them.

Profile

Natalia Corre is the founder of Advance Copy, a consultancy and editorial platform dedicated to supporting the growth of independent fashion brands. With a background at Dries Van Noten and Erdem, she has developed a pragmatic yet human approach to brand development — balancing creative direction, business structure, and long-term well-being. Her method combines strategic clarity with cultural awareness, working with labels such as Cecilie Bahnsen and Neous.

Lecture summary

The lecture explored purpose-driven communication and the role of authenticity and transparency in building sustainable fashion brands. Through the experience of Advance Copy and selected case studies, it showed how clear values can be translated into consistent choices across design, communication, and production, balancing independence and scalability. The talk emphasised the importance of long-term thinking, proposing communication strategies that evolve over time and remain both commercially grounded and culturally conscious.

I personally find Natalia’s approach pragmatic, well-informed, and genuinely inspiring. Her book is a valuable resource for gaining a deeper understanding of many contemporary fashion brands, as well as the strategies and people behind them.

Long-term thinking

The final part of the lecture addressed the importance of long-term thinking: how a brand’s narrative should evolve over time rather than react to trends. Her approach provided a concrete demonstration of what it means to design communication that is both commercially grounded and culturally conscious.

“The design method is nothing more than a series of necessary operations, arranged in a logical order dictated by experience. Its purpose is to achieve the maximum result with the minimum effort.” — B. Munari, Da cosa nasce cosa. Appunti per una metodologia progettuale, Laterza, 1981

Questions

In fashion, how are communication strategies designed? How are visual communication projects developed and managed? How are creative and commercial needs integrated? How are the most effective and innovative contents conceived, planned, and executed? What are the most utilised techniques?

Course focus

Far from being rigid or exhaustive, the course aims to provide high-level professional skills in the conception and development of innovative projects in digital visual communication.

Through the analysis of case histories and the creation of strategic decks, the refinement of aesthetic awareness — crucial in the fashion industry — serves both as a goal and a tool for learning and practicing storytelling and planning techniques.

Structure

The course is divided into three main phases: research, analysis, and design. It begins with research activities for developing communication strategies, followed by the analysis of case histories to study a variety of approaches, from traditional to experimental.

The design phase focuses on applying the acquired tools through a learning-by-doing approach, developing strategic presentations for selected brands.

The visual design and presentation of the projects are developed in collaboration with other lecturers of the course, fostering an integrated and multidisciplinary approach within the Master programme.

Context

Students work on strategic communication decks for fashion brands, balancing research, narrative, and realistic planning.

  • Master in Fashion Digital Marketing — “Project and Methodology of Visual Communication”
  • MA in Fashion Design — “Project and Methodology of Visual Communication”
  • BA in Fashion Design Management — “Multimedia Language · Digital Strategy”

Objectives

  • Master in Fashion Digital Marketing — “Project and Methodology of Visual Communication”
  • MA in Fashion Design — “Project and Methodology of Visual Communication”
  • BA in Fashion Design Management — “Multimedia Language · Digital Strategy”

The course asks for a balance between precision and openness: projects should be structured, but not rigid.

“A method is useful when it can be inhabited and slightly bent, not when it becomes a cage.”
The course is structured in two complementary parts.

Part 1 – Strategy and Storytelling

Project setup, strategic and creative research, definition of the narrative macro-concept, and communication plan. This part is held with Gilda Manfrin.

Part 2 – Realization with AI tools

Content production using digital and AI tools, based on the frameworks developed in the first part. This part is held with other lecturers.

In a landscape marked by content overproduction and the growing impact of digital technologies, the course explores the role of fashion brands as cultural agents — designing communication projects that combine clear strategies, coherent storytelling, and visual direction.

Throughout the course, we analyse contemporary projects and visual references (including Erik Kessels and Penelope Umbrico) to foster critical reflection on the role and evolution of images in visual communication. We focus particularly on emerging brands, while also studying the new creative directions of major fashion houses (Dior, Gucci, Versace, etc.), examining how they use communication to introduce and support recent shifts in creative direction.

AI is used consciously — as a tool for research and idea generation, not as a substitute for reasoning or authorship. A central goal is to strengthen independent research skills and the ability to transform cultural stimuli from the surrounding world into structured project material.

Learning outcomes

  • Develop a complete strategic presentation for a fashion brand, including research, objectives, storytelling, and editorial plan.
  • Set up processes of strategic and creative research to interpret the contemporary landscape and guide project choices.
  • Build a consistent and original narrative framework.
  • Design content typologies and their distribution across formats and platforms.
  • Be prepared for the realization phase with AI tools, with a solid and structured foundation to build on.
“The present is no more than material for the future.”

  2. Why conventional brand-building models no longer apply.

Lecture summary

The lecture explored purpose-driven communication and the role of authenticity and transparency in building sustainable fashion brands. Through the experience of Advance Copy and selected case studies, it showed how clear values can be translated into consistent choices across design, communication, and production, balancing independence and scalability. The talk emphasised the importance of long-term thinking, proposing communication strategies that evolve over time and remain both commercially grounded and culturally conscious.

I personally find Natalia’s approach pragmatic, well-informed, and genuinely inspiring. Her book is a valuable resource for gaining a deeper understanding of many contemporary fashion brands, as well as the strategies and people behind them.

In the context of contemporary communication, characterized by a rapid technological evolution and by an economic uncertainty that also influences creativity, it is essential to provide tools that make it possible to analyze the present and anticipate the languages that will define the future of multimedia media.

Part 1 — Media languages and trends

The first part of the course is focused on studying the main languages and the types of content of social media, as well as on brands’ communication projects. Students are encouraged to engage with examples in an active and critical way, learning to identify future trends rather than simply replicating existing formats.

Part 2 — Digital strategy and editorial thinking

The second part delves into the fundamentals of digital strategy, with particular attention to developing strategic thinking attentive to form, together with the planning of an editorial calendar that connects ideas, formats, and channels over time.

Finally, in the last part of the course, students create a monthly editorial plan for a brand, developing original contents through tools such as artificial intelligence, photography, and video editing.

Through an integrated path between theory and practice, students are encouraged to experiment with a structured and professional approach, transforming the course into a laboratory on the future. The goal is to elaborate personal solutions while exploring the multiplicity of multimedia languages.

Workshop — Thinking and Designing Digital Experiences With (and Without) AI

A two-day inaugural workshop for the Master in Fashion Digital Marketing. It introduced AI not as a production tool, but as a thinking companion — a system for reasoning, structuring, and refining ideas.

Day 1

  • AI as a tool for critical thinking, not just production.
  • Collective discussion: what is a digital experience for a fashion brand today.
  • Keyword selection and conceptual mapping through ChatGPT / Gemini.
  • Visual and conceptual research and analog moodboards.
  • Each group formulated a personal project title from the assigned theme.

Day 2

  • Thematic deepening with prompts for definitions, examples, and guiding questions.
  • Selection of references from art, fashion, and digital culture.
  • Synthesis into insights about today’s digital condition.
  • Ideation of a digital experience and selection of three potential brands.
  • Refinement and final presentations.

Observations

During the workshop, I observed that students were generally able to recount the steps of their process, yet often struggled to connect those steps as parts of a single reasoning flow — as successive moments of one coherent project. This fragmentation is not only methodological but generational.

Jonathan Haidt, in The Anxious Generation (2024), links this to the shift from a “play-based childhood” to a “phone-based childhood” — a transformation that, after 2010, profoundly altered cognitive development. He identifies four main consequences: social deprivation, sleep deprivation, attention fragmentation, and addiction. This “Great Rewiring of Childhood” coincided with a global rise in adolescent anxiety and difficulties in maintaining deep, synthetic thinking.

In this context, the pedagogical challenge is to reactivate the capacity for connection, synthesis, and long-term thinking — helping younger students understand how distinct actions belong to a broader narrative, and how to build projects that endure over time.

Planet Limbo — Fashion as Storytelling of Relational Non-Places

A text you didn’t send. An archived chat. An ambiguous emoji. Someone you ‘love’ who unfollows you. A lover ringing at your door at night saying ‘it’s me’. Friends who wants to be your lover. Matching your forgotten idol on Feeld. Offering an anonymous drink. Being someone erotic’s dream even if you didn’t consent. Talking about someone else’s sexual preferences with your friend. Establishing so many boundaries you can’t do anything you like with them. Feeling intimacy with your Ai girlfriend while in bed with your wife and while sexting with two other people while watching webcams or smart-working. ‘I never saw you in real life but I know your voice and also other parts.’ Waiting for a reply that will never come. Receiving a reply you didn’t really care about.

We live in a world woven with elusive connections, suspended interactions, and bonds whose boundaries are fluid, changing, almost impossible to define precisely. They are situations that absorb and inspire our days, yet we cannot categorize them into clear relational boxes. We don't yet have the right words to fully describe them, because they are constantly evolving, like grains of sand slipping through our fingers or images destined to expire… leaving us in a state of exciting tension and ambiguity.

Our workshop, Planet Limbo, aims to explore this universe of relational ambiguities. Through a series of collaborative sessions, we aim to gather and give form to these elusive experiences. The journey will culminate in the creation of a 24-hour ephemeral exhibition of experimental storytelling. Using fashion as a broad language, we will interpret these themes through diverse media and disciplines, alongside the recovery and transformation of objects.

Clothing touches our bodies, can be forgotten somewhere, can be shared, can be washed, ripped and mended – they are the perfect medium (physically or just conceptually) to represent the visible and invisible threads that connect us.

These elements will become the tools to interpret and narrate the complexities and contradictions of our contemporary relational non-places, offering a space to reflect and share the stories that emerge from this "planet" of undefined connections. Their vagueness and ambiguity might be a new, unusual form of inspiration, romanticism, nostalgia and hidden potential, beyond the most common, generalistic interpretation of gloom, pain and cynicism.

We live in a world woven with elusive connections and ambiguous relational states.

The workshop explores these shifting dynamics through collaborative sessions and storytelling.

Clothing becomes a medium for visible and invisible relational threads.

The goal is to make sense of contemporary relational non-places through experimental interpretation.

Guest Lecture Independent Brands Purpose & Strategy

Background

  • Founder of Advance Copy — consultancy + editorial platform for independent labels.
  • Professional experience at Dries Van Noten and Erdem.
  • Works with brands including Cecilie Bahnsen and Neous.

Core Themes

  • Purpose‑driven communication as a strategic framework.
  • Authenticity and transparency as tools for sustainable growth.
  • Critique of fast‑image / high‑turnover brand models.

Case Studies

  • Kowtow — coherence between design, ethics, and communication.
  • Extreme Cashmere — slow visibility, strong identity.
  • Sincerely Tommy — community‑rooted storytelling.
  • Story Mfg. — value‑driven creative direction.

Key Insight

To build a strong communication strategy, a brand must first possess a clear understanding of its own values and purpose. Without this foundation, strategy becomes decoration rather than direction.

Long‑Term Thinking

Corre highlighted the need for brand narratives that evolve rather than react. Long‑term coherence produces meaning, resilience, and cultural relevance.

Her method combines strategic clarity with cultural awareness, working with labels such as Cecilie Bahnsen and Neous.

Corre opened with the genesis of Advance Copy and its dual role as a consultancy and an editorial platform — a space where strategy and discourse coexist. She argued that conventional brand-building models, based on fast image production and campaign repetition, are increasingly obsolete in a landscape that values slower, more intentional forms of visibility.

Through selected case studies — including Kowtow, Extreme Cashmere, Sincerely Tommy, and Story Mfg. — she illustrated how purpose can be translated into consistent choices across design, communication, and production. Each example served to highlight the tension between independence and scalability, and how clarity of values can become a strategic tool.

To build a proper communication strategy, it is fundamental to work with brands that have a clear understanding of their values and purpose — this is essential to achieve both efficiency and meaning.

The final part of the lecture addressed the importance of long-term thinking: how a brand’s narrative should evolve over time rather than react to trends. Her approach provided a concrete demonstration of what it means to design communication that is both commercially grounded and culturally conscious.
